questions.prompt: A visitor writes one line in the guest book of a school in Sousse: "The pupils looked very smart in their new uniforms." What is she saying about them?

options.text: That they were clever, and answered all her questions.
That they were tidy and well dressed.
That they were quick, and ran when the bell rang.
That they were polite, and stood up when she came in.

questions.explanation: "That they were tidy and well dressed." is the meaning: in this lesson smart describes how a person looks, and the line is about the pupils in their uniforms, that is, about their clothes. "That they were clever, and answered all her questions." borrows the meaning that smart carries in American English, where it does mean clever; your book never uses it that way, and a clever pupil in this lesson is called bright or intelligent. "That they were quick, and ran when the bell rang." confuses smart with a word that names speed, which it does not: nothing in the sentence is about moving fast. And "That they were polite, and stood up when she came in." is about behaviour, but a uniform cannot make anybody polite, and the sentence says in their new uniforms, which points straight at appearance.

questions.prompt: At the end of the lesson a teacher speaks to the whole class about next week's project. Complete what she says: "You will have to organize ___ in groups of four before Thursday."

options.text: yourself
themselves
ourselves
yourselves

questions.explanation: "yourselves" is right: the teacher is speaking to a whole class, so you here means several people, and the plural reflexive ends in -selves. "yourself" is the same pronoun in the singular, for one person only; it is the commonest mistake with this word, because English writes you for one and for many and only the reflexive shows the difference. "themselves" would send the sentence to a third group who are not in the room, while the teacher is addressing the pupils in front of her. And "ourselves" would put the teacher inside the groups of four, which is not what she is asking; she is telling the pupils to organize their own work.

questions.prompt: A note is pinned above the shelves of the school library in El Kef: "Every book you take out is recorded at the desk by the librarian." Which sentence says the same thing to a pupil leaving with a book?

options.text: You needn't write your name in the register.
You mustn't write your name in the register.
You had better not write your name in the register.
You ought not to write your name in the register.

questions.explanation: "You needn't write your name in the register." is the sentence: needn't says that an action is not necessary, and the note gives exactly that reason, since the librarian records every book already. "You mustn't write your name in the register." forbids the action, and the note forbids nothing at all; it simply spares you a gesture. "You had better not write your name in the register." is a warning, and a warning announces something unpleasant if you disobey; the note announces nothing of the kind. And "You ought not to write your name in the register." turns the notice into a duty, as if signing the book out were wrong; it is not wrong, it is only pointless.

questions.prompt: Wassim and Nizar revised together every evening before the exams: whenever one of them lost heart, the other found something encouraging to say to him. Which sentence reports exactly that?

options.text: Wassim and Nizar encouraged themselves every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged them every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged each other every evening.
Wassim and Nizar encouraged theirselves every evening.

questions.explanation: "Wassim and Nizar encouraged each other every evening." is right: each other says that the action crosses between two people, the first encouraging the second and the second encouraging the first, which is precisely what the situation describes. "Wassim and Nizar encouraged themselves every evening." says that each boy encouraged himself, two separate actions with nothing passing between them, so the help they gave each other disappears from the sentence. "Wassim and Nizar encouraged them every evening." sends the encouragement to a third group who are not named anywhere; an object pronoun always points away from the subject. And "Wassim and Nizar encouraged theirselves every evening." uses a word that does not exist in English: the reflexive built on they is themselves, and there is no form theirselves.

questions.prompt: Hedi tells his classmates that he revised the whole night before Saturday's paper and then could not keep his eyes open during the exam. Rania wants to tell him, now that it is all over, that this was the wrong thing to do. Which sentence does she use?

options.text: You shouldn't revise all night before an important exam.
You shouldn't have revised all night before that paper.
You had better not revise all night before your next exam.
You needn't revise all night before an exam like that one.

questions.explanation: "You shouldn't have revised all night before that paper." is the sentence: shouldn't have plus the past participle points at an action that has already been done and says it was the wrong one, which is the reproach Rania wants to make about a night that is over. "You shouldn't revise all night before an important exam." is a present modal, so it advises about the exams still to come and lets the night in question pass without a word. "You had better not revise all night before your next exam." names the next exam itself and warns Hedi about the future, when Rania is speaking about the past. And "You needn't revise all night before an exam like that one." says only that the effort was not necessary, which is not the same judgement: Rania is not telling him he did too much, she is telling him he did something harmful.
